```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 6,
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(geopt)
```

Portugal's boundaries are redrawn from time to time. Data collected before a
change uses the old units, so comparing it with newer data, or putting it on
today's map, requires knowing how the old units relate to the new ones. geopt
calls each version of a set of boundaries a *vintage*.

Three things change, on separate schedules, so geopt tracks each separately:

| What changes | Argument | Vintages |
|---|---|---|
| Freguesias | `admin_vintage` | `"2001"`, `"2011"`, `"2013"`, `"2025"` (current) |
| NUTS regions | `nuts_vintage` | `"2002"`, `"2013"`, `"2024"` (current) |
| Health regions | `health_vintage` | `"2022"`, `"2024"` (current) |

Vintages are always named by their year. If you leave the vintage argument out, the current vintage is returned by default (which may change when geopt adds a newer map). To keep a script's meaning fixed, name the year: `"2025"` will always mean the 2025 map.

Municipalities haven't changed since 1998, so a municipality code means the
same thing in every vintage.

The chart shows when each vintage was in force. Each bar is labelled with the
value to pass, and the number under it is how many units that vintage has
(for NUTS, the number of NUTS 3 regions):

```{r timeline, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 2.8, fig.retina = 2, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.alt = "Timeline from 1995 with one row each for freguesias, NUTS 3 regions and health units, showing the years each vintage was in force."}
library(ggplot2)

n_units <- function(x) length(unique(x))
nuts3 <- function(v) pt_nuts_codes$nuts3_cod[pt_nuts_codes$nuts_vintage == v]

x_min <- 1995
x_max <- 2029

# One bar per vintage, over the years it was in force. A bar with an open start
# is a map with no single start date, and fades in from `start`.
v <- data.frame(
  row = c(3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1),
  label = c("2001", "2011", "2013", "2025", "2002", "2013", "2024", "2022", "2024"),
  start = c(x_min, 2004, 2013, 2025, 2002, 2015, 2024, 2008, 2024),
  end = c(2001.5, 2013, 2025, x_max, 2015, 2024, x_max, 2024, x_max),
  open_start = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE),
  current = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE),
  count = c(
    n_units(pt_lookup(admin_vintage = "2001")$dtmnfr),
    n_units(pt_lookup(admin_vintage = "2011")$dtmnfr),
    n_units(pt_lookup(admin_vintage = "2013")$dtmnfr),
    n_units(pt_lookup(admin_vintage = "2025")$dtmnfr),
    n_units(nuts3("2002")), n_units(nuts3("2013")), n_units(nuts3("2024")),
    n_units(pt_lookup(health_vintage = "2022")$unit),
    n_units(pt_lookup(health_vintage = "2024")$unit)
  )
)

surface <- "#ffffff"
ink <- "#0b0b0b"
muted <- "#52514e"
gap <- 0.1   # half the white gap between neighbouring bars, in years
h <- 0.2     # half the bar height
fade <- 3    # years over which an open start fades in

v$x0 <- ifelse(v$start == x_min, v$start, v$start + gap)
v$x1 <- ifelse(v$end == x_max, v$end, v$end - gap)
v$fill <- ifelse(v$current, "#2a78d6", "#9ec5f4")
v$text_col <- ifelse(v$current, "#ffffff", ink)
solid <- transform(v, x0 = ifelse(open_start, x0 + fade, x0))

# The fade is drawn as thin slices blended from the background to the bar colour
fades <- do.call(rbind, lapply(which(v$open_start), function(i) {
  k <- 24
  edges <- seq(v$x0[i], v$x0[i] + fade, length.out = k + 1)
  mix <- grDevices::colorRamp(c(surface, v$fill[i]))((seq_len(k) - 0.5) / k)
  data.frame(row = v$row[i], x0 = edges[-(k + 1)], x1 = edges[-1] + 0.02,
             fill = grDevices::rgb(mix, maxColorValue = 255))
}))

rows <- data.frame(
  row = 3:1,
  name = c("Freguesias", "NUTS 3 regions", "Health units"),
  arg = c("admin_vintage", "nuts_vintage", "health_vintage")
)

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = x0, xmax = x1, ymin = row - h, ymax = row + h,
                fill = I(fill)), data = fades) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = x0, xmax = x1, ymin = row - h, ymax = row + h,
                fill = I(fill)), data = solid) +
  geom_text(aes(x = x0 + 0.35, y = row, label = paste0('"', label, '"'),
                colour = I(text_col)), data = solid, hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  geom_text(aes(x = x0 + 0.35, y = row - h - 0.13,
                label = format(count, big.mark = ",")),
            data = solid, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, colour = muted, size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(x = x_min - 0.6, y = row + 0.08, label = name), data = rows,
            hjust = 1, colour = ink, size = 3.6, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_text(aes(x = x_min - 0.6, y = row - 0.16, label = arg), data = rows,
            hjust = 1, colour = muted, size = 3, family = "mono") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1995, 2025, 5), minor_breaks = x_min:x_max,
                     expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(add = c(0.45, 0.35))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(x_min, x_max), clip = "off") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "#e1e0d9", linewidth = 0.3),
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_line(colour = "#f0efec", linewidth = 0.25),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(colour = muted),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = surface, colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(8, 12, 4, 118)
  )
```

The darker bars are the current vintages. A vintage's name isn't always the
year it came into force: the 2013 NUTS revision, for example, has been in use
since 2015. Two bars fade in, because those maps have no single start date:
geopt has the freguesias as the 2001 census recorded them, and the health units
as they stood just before the 2024 reform. The gap between the first two
freguesia maps is when new freguesias were being created one at a time (see
below).

This guide covers freguesias and NUTS regions. Health regions have their own
guide, `vignette("health-geographies")`.

## How the freguesias changed

geopt has four freguesia maps:

| `admin_vintage` | In force | Freguesias | Used by | Law |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `"2001"` | until 2001 | 4,241 | the 2001 census | no single law (see below) |
| `"2011"` | 2004 to 2013 | 4,260 | the 2011 census | no single law (see below) |
| `"2013"` | 2013 to 2025 | 3,092 | the 2021 census | Lei 11-A/2013, and Lei 56/2012 for Lisboa |
| `"2025"` | since 2025 | 3,259 | today's official boundaries (CAOP) | Lei 25-A/2025 |

In 2013, about half of all freguesias were merged into *uniões de freguesias*
(unions of freguesias). In 2025, 302 freguesias that had been merged were
restored.

Neither of the maps before 2013 was made by a single law: freguesias were
created one law at a time. So those two maps are named after the census that
recorded them, and the later two after their reform.

Between the two censuses, 22 freguesias were created and 3 dissolved, by laws
of 2001, 2002 and 2003. The 2011 map reached its final form on 1 January 2004,
when the last three came into being: Corvite, Lixa do Alvão and Nossa Senhora
de Fátima (Leis 62/2003, 63/2003 and 68/2003). geopt has the map from before
these changes (`"2001"`) and from after them (`"2011"`), but not the ones in
between.

The 1991 census used an earlier map again, with 4,208 freguesias in 305
municipalities: Odivelas, Trofa and Vizela were only created in 1998. geopt has
no vintage for it.

`pt_crosswalk()` shows how the freguesias of two vintages correspond:

```{r crosswalk}
x <- pt_crosswalk("2013", "2025")
table(x$relation)
```

| `relation` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `unchanged` | same territory, code and name |
| `renamed` | same territory and code, new name |
| `renumbered` | same territory, new code |
| `merged` | several old freguesias became one (the 2013 uniões) |
| `split` | one old freguesia became several (the 2025 restorations) |

For example, the união of Águeda and Borralha became two freguesias again in
2025:

```{r split-example}
x[x$from == "010121", ]
```

The one `renumbered` freguesia is Colos, which kept its territory in 2025 but
got a new code.

**A code only identifies a freguesia within its own vintage.** None of the
freguesias restored in 2025 got its pre-2013 code back. Don't join data from
one vintage onto codes from another: go through `pt_crosswalk()` or
`pt_recode()`.

## Bringing older data onto today's map

`pt_recode()` converts a data frame from one vintage to another. What it
should do with the values depends on the direction, and on what kind of value
they are:

| | Counts (cases, population) | Rates, averages, medians |
|---|---|---|
| Several old freguesias become one | add them up: `aggregate = sum` | can't be combined: convert the counts, then recompute |
| One old freguesia becomes several | share them out: `split = "weight"` | copy to each: `split = "replicate"` |

`pt_recode()` won't guess. It stops if a merge happens without `aggregate`, or
a split without `split`.

### From the 2013 map: splits

Data from 2013 to 2025, such as the 2021 census, has one value per união.
Some uniões are several freguesias now, and there's no exact way to divide a
value between them, so choose how:

```{r split}
old <- data.frame(dtmnfr = "010121", casos = 100)

# Copy the value to every restored freguesia (right for rates)
pt_recode(old, from = "2013", values = "casos", split = "replicate")

# Share it out in proportion to area
pt_recode(old, from = "2013", values = "casos",
          split = "weight", weights = "area")
```

Area is a rough guide, because people don't spread out evenly. If a better
weight is available, such as population, pass it as a named vector keyed by
the current code:

```{r split-pop, eval = FALSE}
pop <- c("010130" = 14000, "010133" = 5000)  # population per freguesia
pt_recode(old, from = "2013", values = "casos",
          split = "weight", weights = pop)
```

### From before 2013: mostly merges

Going from the pre-2013 map to today is mostly the opposite: several old
freguesias now form one união, so their counts are added up. These three old
freguesias of Anadia are one freguesia today:

```{r pre2013-recode}
old <- data.frame(dtmnfr = c("010301", "010302", "010314"),
                  pop = c(500, 800, 300))
pt_recode(old, from = "2011", values = "pop", aggregate = sum)
```

Not every old freguesia was merged. Many are unchanged, and those restored in
2025 match a current freguesia one to one:

```{r pre2013}
x11 <- pt_crosswalk("2011", "2025")
table(x11$relation)
```

If the data has only some members of a união, the total covers the ones
present, and a warning says the group is incomplete.

### When only names are available

People working with older files often have only freguesia names but no codes. `name_from` holds the name each freguesia had at the time, which is usually not today's name:

```{r pre2013-names}
x11[x11$to == "030364", c("from", "name_from", "name_to")]
```

`pt_match()` recognizes these older names, and returns the freguesia that
covers the same place today:

```{r pre2013-forward}
old <- data.frame(freg = c("Sé", "Maximinos", "Cividade", "Gualtar"),
                  mun = "Braga", pop = c(100, 200, 300, 400))
old$dtmnfr <- pt_match(old$freg, level = "freguesia", context = old$mun,
                        quiet = TRUE)
old
```

The first three were merged in 2013, so they now share one code. Add them up
before joining:

```{r pre2013-aggregate}
aggregate(pop ~ dtmnfr, old, sum)
```

To get the code each freguesia had before 2013 instead, pass
`admin_vintage = "2011"`. Each old freguesia then keeps its own code, and
`pt_recode()` can convert the data from there:

```{r pre2013-own}
d <- data.frame(dtmnfr = pt_match(old$freg, level = "freguesia",
                                   context = old$mun, admin_vintage = "2011",
                                   quiet = TRUE),
                pop = old$pop)
d
pt_recode(d, from = "2011", values = "pop", aggregate = sum)
```

With `admin_vintage = "2011"`, a *current* name only matches if that freguesia
had a single predecessor. A união that absorbed several returns `NA`, because
nothing says which of them was meant.

### Data from the 2001 census

Most freguesias of the 2001 map are the same in 2011, with the same code. The
exceptions are 17: 3 that were dissolved, and 14 that gave up part of their
territory to a new freguesia but kept their code. In 2001, for example, Ponte
(Guimarães) still included Corvite:

```{r ponte}
x01 <- pt_crosswalk("2001", "2011")
x01[x01$from == "030838", ]
```

So a value for Ponte in 2001 data covers two freguesias of the 2011 map. With
`from = "2001"`, `pt_recode()` treats it as the split it is; read as 2011 data,
all of it would silently go to the smaller Ponte:

```{r ponte-recode}
pt_recode(data.frame(dtmnfr = "030838", taxa = 4.2), from = "2001",
          to = "2011", values = "taxa", split = "replicate")
```

Names work the same way: with `admin_vintage = "2001"`, `pt_match()` returns
the 2001 code, and it matches names that were gone by 2011, such as
Agualva-Cacém.

The 2001 census areas from `get_censos()` give two freguesias a different code
from INE's own list, because both had moved to another municipality: Vale de
Amoreira (`090756` instead of `090804`) and Moita (`100117` instead of
`101003`). `pt_recode()` and `pt_match()` accept both codes for `"2001"`.

### The other way: today's data on the 2013 map

To compare current data with the 2021 census, convert it back to the 2013 map.
The restored freguesias go back into their união, so this is a merge:

```{r merge}
members <- x$to[x$from == "010121"]
df <- data.frame(dtmnfr = members, casos = c(30, 10))

pt_recode(df, from = "2025", to = "2013", values = "casos", aggregate = sum)
```

## Maps of another vintage

`get_map()` draws the 2025 map. `admin_vintage = "2013"` draws the map in force
from the 2013 reform until the 2025 restorations, from DGT's official
boundaries (CAOP 2024, the last release on that map). The first call downloads
and simplifies them, which takes a few minutes and needs the rmapshaper
package. After that the result is cached, so later calls take seconds:

```{r year-map, eval = FALSE}
m2013 <- get_map("freguesia", admin_vintage = "2013")
sum(m2013$geopt_type == "boundary")   # 3092 freguesias
```

Data on the 2013 map then goes straight onto it, without converting. Names are
matched against the 2013 freguesias, so that map's uniões are found by name:

```{r year-map-join, eval = FALSE}
get_map("freguesia", admin_vintage = "2013", data = data_2021, by = "dtmnfr")
```

Each 2013 freguesia has the last name it carried on that map, the one INE
publishes. Names it had earlier match as well:

```{r names-2013}
pt_match(c("Buarcos e São Julião", "Buarcos"), level = "freguesia",
         context = "Figueira da Foz", admin_vintage = "2013", quiet = TRUE)
```

Both are `060520`: the freguesia was called Buarcos until it was renamed in
2015.

`nuts_vintage` does the same for NUTS: `get_map("nuts3", nuts_vintage = "2013")`
draws the 25 NUTS 3 regions of the 2013 revision, from the bundled data, with
nothing to download. Any NUTS revision combines with either freguesia map,
because every revision groups whole municipalities. The health levels exist on
the 2025 map only.

`get_map()` doesn't draw the maps from before 2013. For boundaries of that
era, download the census areas with `get_censos()`.
Their `dtmnfr` column holds the code of that census's map (`"2011"` for
2011, `"2001"` for 2001), so they can be merged into freguesias:

```{r censos-2011, eval = FALSE}
bgri <- get_censos(region = "ram", year = 2011,
                   variables = "N_INDIVIDUOS_RESIDENT")
freg_2011 <- aggregate(bgri["N_INDIVIDUOS_RESIDENT"],
                       by = list(dtmnfr = bgri$dtmnfr), FUN = sum)
```

## NUTS regions

The NUTS regions are groups of municipalities, and they're revised every few
years. geopt has three revisions:

| `nuts_vintage` | In use | NUTS 3 regions | Law |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"2002"` | 2002 to 2015 | 30 | Decreto-Lei 244/2002 |
| `"2013"` | 2015 to 2024 | 25 | Regulation (EU) 868/2014 |
| `"2024"` | since 2024 | 26 | Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/674 |

Because they're built from municipalities, `pt_nuts_codes` lists each
municipality's region in every revision. Covilhã, for example, moved to a new
NUTS 3 region in 2013:

```{r nuts-revisions}
pt_nuts_codes[pt_nuts_codes$dtmn == "0503", c("nuts_vintage", "nuts3_cod", "nuts3")]
```

`pt_lookup(nuts_vintage = )` gives the whole table for one revision.

The NUTS revision is independent of the freguesia map. INE publishes the same
freguesias under more than one NUTS revision, so choose `nuts_vintage` and
`admin_vintage` separately.

### Matching NUTS names: say which revision

`pt_match()` matches NUTS names against the current revision unless told
otherwise. Some older names cover territory that is split between several
regions today, so they aren't matched. The 2002 region of Tâmega, for example,
is spread across four of today's NUTS 3 regions:

```{r nuts-old-name}
pt_match(c("Tâmega", "Alto Trás-os-Montes"), level = "nuts3", quiet = TRUE)

pt_match(c("Tâmega", "Alto Trás-os-Montes"), level = "nuts3",
         nuts_vintage = "2002", quiet = TRUE)
```

The riskier case is a name that both revisions use for different areas. It
matches today's region, with no sign that the area has changed:

```{r nuts-shared-name}
pt_match("Ave", level = "nuts3", quiet = TRUE)                        # today's Ave
pt_match("Ave", level = "nuts3", nuts_vintage = "2002", quiet = TRUE) # the 2002 Ave
```

Five NUTS 3 names are used by both the 2002 and current revisions for
different groups of municipalities:

```{r nuts-shared-table}
n <- pt_nuts_codes
members <- function(v, nm) sort(n$dtmn[n$nuts_vintage == v & n$nuts3 == nm])

shared <- intersect(n$nuts3[n$nuts_vintage == "2002"],
                    n$nuts3[n$nuts_vintage == "2024"])
moved <- Filter(function(nm) !identical(members("2002", nm), members("2024", nm)),
                shared)
moved
```

So when matching the regions in an INE series, check which NUTS revision the
series uses, and pass it as `nuts_vintage`. Of the 28 NUTS 3 names INE
publishes under "NUTS - 2002", 22 match without `nuts_vintage`, but only to
today's regions of the same name. With it, all 28 match the right 2002
regions.
